Connect to foundations: The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Track the second derivative of size along each direction Different directions can require different support even at the same total energy. Differentiate the inertia tensor twice and use continuity and Euler’s equation. For an unmagnetized fluid with zero surface pressure: Iᵢⱼ = ∫ρxᵢxⱼdV, Tᵢⱼ = 12∫ρvᵢvⱼdV 12Ïᵢⱼ = 2Tᵢⱼ+Wᵢⱼ+Πδᵢⱼ Wᵢⱼ = −∫ρxᵢ∂Φ∂xⱼdV, Π=∫PdV Taking the trace recovers the scalar virial theorem. Random orbital stresses enter a stellar system; here Π represents fluid pressure. Do not double count these supports. 02Insert the homogeneous ellipsoid Iᵢᵢ = Maᵢ²5, Wᵢᵢ = −2πGρAᵢIᵢᵢ Φeff = Φ−Ω²2(x²+y²) A uniformly rotating incompressible fluid obeys P/ρ + Φeff = constant in its rotating frame. Zero pressure at the surface requires equal effective potentials at the three axis endpoints. (A₁−ω²/2)a²=(A₂−ω²/2)b²=A₃c², ω² ≡ Ω²πGρ A Jacobi figure rotates in the inertial frame: Ï₁₁ = 2Ω²(I₂₂−I₁₁), rather than zero. Including this term recovers the same surface condition. A fixed shape in a rotating frame need not have fixed inertial tensor components. 03Maclaurin: an axisymmetric sequence For a = b, q = c/a and e = √(1−q²), the two equatorial conditions coincide. Use the previous chapter’s coefficients to obtain angular speed. ω²=2(A₁−q²A₃) = 2√(1−e²)e³[(3−2e²)sin−1e−3e√(1−e²)] At small e, ω² ≈ (8/15)e², so the spherical limit has zero rotation. Angular speed does not grow monotonically forever with flattening; it need not uniquely identify a figure. 04Jacobi: solve a triaxial sequence Set a = 1 and use p = b/a and q = c/a. Eliminate ω² between the equatorial conditions. The panel integrates Aᵢ and bisects for q at each specified p. A₂−A₁p−2−1=A₃q², ω²=2(A₁−A₃q²) As a reference check, Fitzpatrick Table 2.2 gives e₁₃ ≈ 0.85585 and Ω/√(2πGρ) ≈ 0.42827 at e₁₂ = 0.6, or b/a = 0.8. The panel uses Ω²/(πGρ); divide by two and take its square root before comparing to that table. The two controls select independent equilibria, not an equal-angular-momentum pair. These are calculated equilibrium sequences, not a time-dependent transformation from one fluid shape to another. 05Bifurcation and two kinds of instability The Jacobi branch bifurcates near e = 0.81267 and T/|W| = 0.1375. Weak-viscosity secular instability differs from the ideal-fluid dynamical bar instability near e = 0.95289 and T/|W| = 0.2738. These thresholds are supplied perturbation results. T=MΩ²(a²+b²)10, W=−2πGρM5ΣAᵢaᵢ² Solving equilibrium does not prove stability. Compressibility, differential rotation, fields, relativity and collisionless dynamics change the problem. No stability claim is made for the entire Jacobi branch; these plots recompute equilibrium equations, not all paper curves or perturbation eigenvalues. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At e = 0.85 on the homogeneous Maclaurin sequence, distinguish weak-viscosity instability from dynamical instability. Show the answer and reasoning It lies above the secular threshold 0.81267 but below the dynamical bar-mode threshold 0.95289. These are perturbation results for a homogeneous incompressible fluid, not universal rotating-star thresholds. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text.
